title: Out-of-pocket medical costs 'up 28pc'
full_text:
One of the country's biggest private health funds, Bupa, says out-of-pocket costs for its 4 million members have surged more than 28 per cent in the past two years due to skyrocketing specialist doctor fees and other healthcare costs.
Bupa's submission to a parliamentary inquiry into specialist doctor fees highlights soaring healthcare costs and says people are delaying or skipping specialist care because they can't afford it. The Albanese government wants to make specialist doctor fees more transparent or cap them as it seeks to fulfil a second-term election pledge to lower the cost of healthcare.
Out-of-pocket costs in health insurance are the amounts patients have to pay themselves because they are not reimbursed by Medicare or a private health fund. Bupa said 60 per cent of patients admitted to private hospitals were paying out-of-pocket costs.
For most patients, those costs were $500 or more but for certain procedures it can be thousands of dollars. For an uncomplicated hip replacement, the median out-of-pocket medical cost was about $1448.29.
The cost of seeing a specialist like a psychiatrist, dermatologist, paediatrician or oncologist outside a hospital setting is not covered by Medicare or private health insurance and typically costs hundreds of dollars per appointment. Bupa, the country's biggest health fund alongside Medibank Private, said its data showed 8.6 per cent of Australians delayed or skipped specialist care in the 2025 fiscal year because they could not afford it.
In total, 18.3 per cent deferred or did not see a specialist when needed, with other factors such as high wait times and lack of availability also a problem, the insurer said.
Bupa's submission, which will be made public on Monday, said members complained of long wait times to see specialist doctors, with some patients in rural and regional areas waiting up to 258 days to see a psychiatrist.
Its submission highlighted workforce shortages as well as doctors working shorter hours than before the COVID-19 pandemic, which was making it harder to get an appointment.
"Rising out-of-pocket costs, limited transparency about fees and constrained access to publicly funded specialist services are making it more difficult for patients to obtain timely care," Bupa said in its submission, which stopped short of calling for a cap on specialist fees.
Data from the Medical Cost Finder tool shows that patients who had an initial specialist consultation in 2025 typically paid $147 in out-of-pocket costs, with 10 per cent of patients paying $252 or more for a single appointment.
Costs vary across and within specialties, from $100-$307 for an initial paediatric consultation, to $173-$503 for an initial psychiatry consultation, according to Bupa.
Fees also varied hugely across regions and specialities. Gap fees were $100 to $307 for paediatrics and up to $500 for a visit to a psychiatrist. The ACT had median out-of-pocket costs of $591 per appointment, more than double the national median of $240.
Health Minister Mark Butler has said reducing specialists' fees is a second-term priority for the Albanese government. The government has referred the matter to a parliamentary inquiry that is due to report later this month. Submissions to that inquiry close on Friday.
Submissions to a second Health Department inquiry looking at options to address excessive fees close on Monday. The Albanese government has indicated there is a strong case for the government to intervene on fees.
However, the move threatens a showdown with doctors, who argue fees must vary as some cases are more complex than others and Medicare rebates have failed to keep up with inflation.
"When rebates and insurer benefits fail to keep pace with the cost of delivering care, patients shoulder more of the expense. Publishing a fee makes it visible. It does not make an inadequate rebate sufficient," said Vida Viliunas, president of the Australian Society of Anaesthetists.
"Government should examine Medicare indexation and insurers' no-gap and known-gap arrangements with the same seriousness it applies to specialist charging. Transparency and accountability must extend to everyone whose decisions determine what patients pay."
